Atlantic tripletail (Lobotes surinamensis) is a large-bodied, warm-water predator that inhabits estuarine and coastal waters of the Atlantic Ocean. During the incubation period, eggs maintained at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] hatch after just a single day (1 day) [ab = 1 day], a remarkably short duration that reflects the elevated metabolic rates typical of tropical teleost embryos. This rapid eclosion yields extremely small yolk-sac larvae, with an initial wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000065 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000065 grams], a mass consistent with the species' buoyant, pelagic eggs that measure roughly 0.5 mm in diameter. Following hatching, the prolarvae absorb their endogenous yolk reserves quickly, transitioning to exogenous feeding within hours, as the mouth gapes open and retinal differentiation enables prey detection. The abbreviated incubation period and diminutive neonate mass place Lobotes surinamensis at the fast end of the life-history spectrum among percoid fishes, where a high reproductive output is traded against minimal parental investment per offspring. This developmental strategy is well suited to the productive, predator-rich surface waters of its subtropical nursery habitats.

Field surveys and growth-curve analyses have provided robust estimates of body size at key life-history transitions for this species. Females of Atlantic tripletail attain puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal maturation, at a total length of 48.5 centimeters [Lp = 48.5 centimeters], a considerably larger size than that observed in males, which reach sexual maturation at a total length of 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation size is unusual among teleosts and likely reflects divergent selective pressures on the two sexes, with females benefiting from the increased fecundity that accompanies a larger body cavity and greater somatic reserves. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 2624 grams [Wwp = approximately 2624 grams], whereas males invest in reproductive activation at a markedly lower body mass of approximately 609 grams [Wwp = approximately 609 grams], a difference that underscores the energetic constraints on vitellogenesis and egg production relative to the modest costs of spermatogenesis. This pattern of size dimorphism at puberty is among the most extreme documented for percoid fishes and indicates strong fecundity selection acting on females, as a larger abdominal cavity accommodates greater ovarian mass and thus higher potential fecundity.

Analysis of specimens from commercial and recreational fisheries reveals that Atlantic tripletail reaches a maximum total length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters], making it one of the largest members of the family Lobotidae. The corresponding ultimate wet weight derived from length-weight regressions is approximately 26853 grams [Wwi = approximately 26853 grams], a mass that positions the species as a formidable apex predator within its estuarine and shelf-zone habitats. Comparisons with related percoid fishes indicate that this asymptotic size is consistent with a moderately slow growth trajectory once maturity is attained, though juvenile growth rates can be quite rapid under favorable thermal and prey conditions. The length-weight relationship used to estimate adult mass—fitted from a large dataset of landed individuals—shows an exponent close to 2.84, suggesting a slightly negative allometric growth pattern in which heavier individuals become somewhat more elongate relative to their mass. This allometric shift is typical of species that occupy pelagic feeding niches as adults, where maneuverability may be prioritized over volumetric capacity.

Reproductive output in Atlantic tripletail has been quantified through gravimetric analysis of ovaries from ripe females collected during the spawning season. At a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a female measuring approximately 61 centimeters in total length produces around 22000 eggs per day [Ri = around 22000 eggs per day], with the spawning period extending over several months. The total annual egg production, equivalent to roughly 8 million eggs over a 365-day cycle, is consistent with a single prolonged spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 8 million eggs over a 365-day cycle, is consistent with a single prolonged spawning event] that occurs once per year [F_R_i = once per year]. This daily reproductive rate is among the highest recorded for a fish of comparable mass and reflects a classic r-selected reproductive strategy typical of warm-water species with high larval mortality. Field observations indicate that spawning occurs in aggregations over the continental shelf, with peak activity coinciding with summer temperature maxima. The prolonged daily egg production, sustained over a multi-month season, allows tripletail to exploit ephemeral oceanographic conditions that enhance larval survival, such as warm-core rings and frontal zones that concentrate planktonic prey for the exogenously feeding larvae after the yolk-sac stage.

Longevity estimates for Atlantic tripletail, derived from otolith-based age determinations, indicate that individuals can live for up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years] when maintained under ambient thermal regimes typical of subtropical waters at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This maximum lifespan, equivalent to roughly 3650 days, is moderate for a teleost of its ultimate body size; many comparably large percoids exhibit longer lifespans, suggesting that the species' fast growth and early maturation may come at a cost of reduced somatic durability or increased vulnerability to senescence. The age-length key constructed from otolith readings reveals that growth slows markedly after the onset of sexual maturity, with the majority of somatic mass accumulation occurring within the first three to five years. This early-life growth strategy aligns with the species' ecological role as a transient predator that must reach a size refuge from gape-limited predators quickly. In contrast to longer-lived percoids such as the white seabass, which may exceed 20 years, the 10-year (10 years) [am = 10 years] longevity of Atlantic tripletail at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] is consistent with its higher metabolic rate and faster early growth, making it a relatively short-lived species within its family.
